messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Alvarez was 36 when he came for treatment, a psychiatrist who had spent years moving efficiently through hospital corridors and speaking calmly with frightened families. The event that undid that ordinary competence centered on his young nephew, a child he had helped raise and who shared his first name as a middle name, so that hearing it spoken had once felt affectionate and familiar. Two years earlier, the boy became critically ill with a sudden, life-threatening infection. Mateo drove behind the ambulance to the emergency department through city traffic, listening to the rise and fall of sirens and the uneven rush of passing cars, and when he reached the hospital he was met by the sharp smell of alcohol from hand sanitizer, wipes, and the child’s skin being cleaned for procedures. What stayed with him most was not a coherent sequence but sensory fragments: the child’s name shouted across the room, monitors and traffic outside the ambulance bay, and that antiseptic-alcohol smell saturating everything.

In the weeks afterward, Mateo found that these fragments did not settle into an ordinary memory. At times he could describe the admission with a flat, detached precision that embarrassed him; he sounded, even to himself, as if he were presenting someone else’s case. At other moments the memory surged back with such force that he had to cut it off mid-thought, his chest tightening and his mind flooding too quickly to continue. When it returned, he did not just think about that night—he heard it. A car accelerating outside his apartment or the layered sounds of traffic near the hospital parking garage could bring back the remembered noise in his head, as if he were again chasing the ambulance and straining to catch the shouted updates.

Those sensory reminders began to organize his days more than he liked to admit. In the hospital where he worked, hearing his nephew’s name—or a similar one called out on a pediatric consult, in the waiting room, or even in casual conversation—could abruptly pull him toward the worst moments of that night. The smell of alcohol gel outside patient rooms and the churn of cars near the emergency entrance did the same. Once stirred, the memory came in pieces: a numb recounting one hour, then an unbearable rush the next, along with the internal echo of voices and vehicle noise. He started avoiding the emergency department unless absolutely necessary, and if a colleague asked whether he could cover a consult involving ambulances, physical examination in a high-acuity setting, or a family waiting near intensive care, he found ways to hand it off. He told himself this was practical, but he knew he was steering away from hospitals within his own hospital.

When reminders caught him and the memory pressed close, Mateo tried to get out from under it by shifting into agitation. After a difficult day he would pick an argument with his sister about minor decisions, or bait a colleague in a case conference over some small point of judgment, feeling a brief, ugly relief when the focus turned to anger instead of helplessness. He also became preoccupied with fantasies of getting even with the man he believed had delayed seeking medical care for the child and then minimized how sick he was. Mateo would run through imagined confrontations in his head, rehearsing what he would say, how he would expose his negligence, how he would make him feel the panic he had caused. The more often he was jarred by a name, by traffic, by alcohol on the air, the more he reached for conflict or these revenge-laden loops to keep from being dragged back into the rawness of the memory.

Yet the memory also made the world feel crowded with reminders. Because it returned as sounds and isolated sensory flashes rather than as a fully past event, ordinary car noise outside his office no longer felt neutral. Hearing his nephew’s name at work did not stay a word; it became charged, expectant. The alcohol smell on his own hands after sanitizing could stop him in a hallway. He had come to watch for these moments, bracing before rounds, choosing stairs instead of the ambulance entrance, delaying examinations he would once have done without hesitation. The habits accumulated consequences. Colleagues noticed that he was harder to work with and strangely unavailable around medical crises; his sister had begun limiting contact because every conversation seemed to tilt into accusation or drama.

What finally brought Mateo in was a recent incident in which a child patient in consultation shared his nephew’s name. He froze, heard the remembered sounds roaring in his head, and had to step out before the interview was finished. Later, numb and ashamed, he picked a fight with a coworker over documentation and spent the drive home replaying what he would do to the man he blamed for the original ordeal. He sought help because he was frightened by how narrow his life had become inside the very hospital where he worked, and because what he wanted most was to hear a child’s name, smell sanitizer, or pass the ambulance bay without feeling as if that night were happening again.
